learn.b: HTML is the language that gives a web page its structure. It is made of elements written with tags in angle brackets. Most elements have an opening tag, content and a closing tag with a slash.

Every page starts with a doctype that tells the browser it is modern HTML. The html element wraps everything. Inside, head holds information about the page like its title, and body holds what people see.

Attributes give extra information to an element. They go inside the opening tag as name="value". Examples are lang on html and charset on meta. Some elements, like meta and img, are void and have no closing tag.

Elements can sit inside other elements, which is called nesting. Close the inner element before the outer one. Comments start with <!-- and end with -->, and the browser does not show them. Indenting your code makes the structure easy to read.

learn.b: Headings go from h1, the main title, to h6, the smallest. Use one h1 per page and keep the order sensible. The p element makes a paragraph, and the browser adds space around it.
Use strong for important text, which is usually bold. Use em for stressed text, which is usually italic. They carry meaning, not only looks. The b and i tags only change how text looks.
The br tag makes a line break inside a paragraph, and hr draws a horizontal line. Both are void elements with no closing tag. Extra spaces and new lines in your code are collapsed into one space.

Use blockquote for a long quote and q for a short one. code shows computer code, and pre keeps spaces and line breaks. span and div are generic containers with no meaning: span is inline and div is block.

learn.b: The a element makes a link. Its href attribute holds the address to open, and the content is the clickable text. Use a full address for other sites and a file name for pages on your own site.
Add target="_blank" to open a link in a new tab, together with rel="noopener" for safety. A link starting with # jumps to the element with that id on the same page. mailto: opens an email.

learn.b: The img tag shows a picture. The src attribute is the file path or address, and alt is a text description. alt is read by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. Set width and height to avoid the page jumping while loading.

A relative path is found from the current page, like images/dog.jpg, or ../logo.png to go up one folder. An absolute path is a full address starting with https. An image can be inside a link to make it clickable. Use figure and figcaption to add a caption.

learn.b: Use ul for an unordered list with bullets and ol for an ordered list with numbers. Each item goes in a li element. Lists can be nested by putting a new list inside an li.
A dl element makes a list of terms and descriptions. The dt element is the term and dd is its description. This is useful for glossaries.
A table is built from rows. The table element wraps tr rows, and each row has td cells. Use th for header cells, which are bold and centered by default. Tables are for data, not for page layout.

Group rows with thead, tbody and tfoot, and add a caption to name the table. colspan and rowspan let a cell stretch across columns or rows. Use scope on th so screen readers know whether it heads a column or a row.

learn.b: A form collects information from a visitor. The action attribute says where the data goes and method says how, usually get or post. Inside the form you place inputs and a submit button.

The input element changes with its type attribute: text, email, password, number, checkbox, radio, date and more. Always connect a label to its input with for and id, so clicking the label focuses the field. The name attribute is the key of the sent data.
textarea is for many lines of text. select with option elements makes a drop-down list. Radio buttons share the same name so only one can be chosen. A checkbox can be ticked on its own.
learn.code:
<textarea name="msg" rows="3"></textarea>
<select name="color">
  <option value="r">Red</option>
  <option value="b">Blue</option>
</select>
<input type="radio" name="size" value="s"> Small

learn.b: Attributes like required, min, max, minlength and pattern let the browser check input before sending. placeholder shows a hint inside an empty field. Group related fields with fieldset and name the group with legend.
learn.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Account</legend>
  <input type="password" name="pw" minlength="8" placeholder="8+ characters" required>
</fieldset>

learn.b: Semantic elements describe their meaning, not only their look. Use header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer instead of generic divs. Search engines and screen readers use them to understand the page.
Use one main per page, and one h1 as the main heading. Headings should not skip levels, like going from h2 to h5. A section needs a heading. aside holds side information such as related links.

Every meaningful image needs alt text that explains what it shows. A purely decorative image gets an empty alt, alt="". Every form input needs a label. Link text should make sense alone, so avoid "click here".

learn.b: CSS controls how HTML looks: colors, sizes, spacing and layout. A rule has a selector that picks elements and a block of declarations in curly braces. Each declaration is a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon.

The best way is a separate file linked from head with a link element. You can also put rules inside a style element, or use the style attribute on one element. A separate file lets many pages share the same look.
learn.code: Hi

learn.b: An element selector uses the tag name like p. A class selector starts with a dot and picks every element with that class. An id selector starts with # and should be used once per page. The star * picks everything.

A comma picks several selectors at once. A space picks descendants, so nav a means links inside nav. A > picks direct children only. Pseudo-classes like :hover and :first-child pick elements in a special state or position. When rules conflict, the more specific one wins, then the later one.

learn.b: Color names like red work, but you can also use hex codes like #ff0000, rgb(255, 0, 0), or hsl(0, 100%, 50%). Hex and rgb mix red, green and blue. Add alpha with rgba for see-through colors. color sets text color and background-color sets the background.

font-family lists fonts in order of preference, ending with a generic family like sans-serif or serif. font-size can be in px, em or rem. rem is relative to the root size, so it scales well. Put names with spaces in quotes.

font-weight sets how bold text is, with normal, bold or numbers like 700. font-style: italic slants text. text-align aligns text to left, center or right. line-height sets the space between lines, and text-decoration adds underlines.

Google Fonts and @font-face let you use fonts the visitor does not have installed. Link the font or declare it, then use its name in font-family. Always keep a fallback generic family. Keep text color and background at strong contrast so it is easy to read.

learn.b: The browser draws every element as a rectangle with four layers. From the inside out they are content, padding, border and margin. Padding is space inside the border, and margin is space outside it.

With one value, all four sides get it. With two values, the first is top and bottom and the second is left and right. With four values they go clockwise: top, right, bottom, left. You can also set one side, like margin-top.
learn.code:
padding: 10px;            /* all sides */
padding: 10px 20px;       /* top-bottom left-right */
margin: 1px 2px 3px 4px;  /* top right bottom left */
margin-top: 8px;

learn.b: border sets width, style and color together. border-radius rounds the corners. By default width only covers the content, so padding and border make the box bigger. Setting box-sizing: border-box includes them in the width, which is much easier to plan.

Block elements like div and p start on a new line and fill the width. Inline elements like span and a sit in the text and ignore width and height. inline-block mixes both. margin: 0 auto centers a block with a set width. Vertical margins of neighbors can collapse into one.

learn.b: Set display: flex on a parent and its children become flex items laid out in a row. The parent is the container. Items can shrink or grow to fit. It makes one dimensional layouts, a row or a column, easy.

flex-direction sets the main axis: row (default) or column. flex-wrap: wrap lets items move onto new lines when there is no space. The main axis follows the direction and the cross axis runs across it.

justify-content spreads items along the main axis with values like center, space-between and flex-end. align-items aligns them along the cross axis with values like center and stretch. gap adds space between items. To center something perfectly use both justify-content and align-items set to center.

flex-grow tells an item how much extra space to take. flex: 1 makes items share space equally. flex-basis sets the starting size, and align-self lets one item align differently. order changes the visual position.

learn.b: Set display: grid on a parent to make a two dimensional layout with rows and columns. You define the columns with grid-template-columns. Children fill the cells automatically.
fr is a fraction of the free space. 1fr 2fr gives the second column twice as much space. repeat(3, 1fr) is a short way to write three equal columns. Use grid-template-rows to size rows the same way.
grid-column and grid-row place an item by line numbers. span makes an item cover several cells. Lines are numbered from 1. gap, column-gap and row-gap set the space between cells.

grid-template-areas names regions of the layout like a map, and each item uses grid-area with its name. For responsive cards without media queries use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)). Grid is for whole page layouts and flexbox is for single rows or columns.

learn.b: Phones pretend to be wide unless you tell them otherwise. Add the viewport meta tag in head so the page uses the real screen width. Without it your responsive CSS will not work on phones.

Avoid fixed pixel widths for layout. Use percentages, max-width and relative units like rem. Images should never be wider than their container, so use max-width: 100% and height: auto. Flexbox with wrap and grid with auto-fit adapt without extra rules.

A media query applies CSS only if a condition is true, such as the screen being narrow. min-width queries apply from a size and up, and max-width queries apply up to a size. Common breakpoints are around 600px and 900px, but choose them where your design breaks.

Mobile first means writing the small screen styles first, then adding min-width queries for larger screens. It keeps phone CSS simple and fast. You can also query by orientation or by a dark color scheme preference. Test by resizing the browser or using the device mode in the developer tools.
